claims.text: Thermal exposure causes diffusion-driven Mg segregation to grain boundaries in a metastable Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy.
Grain-boundary Mg segregation preferentially nucleates intermetallic compounds.
Fine, nascent intermetallic regions support formation of a coherent protective oxide layer.
The oxide layer associated with fine intermetallics preserves corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance under moderate service conditions.
Continued aging or exposure at higher temperature causes intermetallic compounds to coarsen and interconnect.
Coarsened, interconnected intermetallic phases disrupt oxide-scale continuity.
Disruption of oxide-scale continuity accelerates corrosion and oxidation degradation.
Moderate-temperature or short-duration aging will produce fine grain-boundary intermetallic precipitates.
Moderate-temperature or short-duration aging will leave the oxide layer largely intact and preserve resistance relative to the initial state.
Higher-temperature or prolonged aging will produce an interconnected network of coarse intermetallic phases.
Higher-temperature or prolonged aging will yield disrupted oxide morphology and accelerated corrosion or oxidation.
The initial alloy has a uniform metastable solid-solution microstructure.
Service below approximately 600 °C is expected to retain a protective oxide layer.
Service above approximately 700 °C, or for sufficiently long durations, is expected to promote intermetallic coarsening and degrade resistance.
The exact Mg-diffusion kinetics and competition between protective oxide formation and intermetallic coarsening are not characterized.
Introducing an additional minor element can sequester Mg and inhibit its grain-boundary segregation.
The oxidation behavior and oxide phases of a high-entropy alloy can change with exposure temperature and atmosphere.
